guide.title: Prati, Rome: the Palazzaccio, a Caryatid Fountain and the Only Rione Outside the Walls
guide.intro: Prati is the twenty-second and last of Rome's rioni, and it lies outside the city walls - outside the Aurelian, the Gianicolensi and the Leonine circuits alike. Roma Capitale's Annuario statistico 2022 gives it the toponymic code 122; Italian Wikipedia's table of the rioni, citing comune.roma.it, records 14,631 residents on 1.2743 square kilometres. It is a made quarter rather than a grown one: flood-plain known as Prati di Castello into the 1880s, laid out on a grid after a building convention of 1873, and constituted a rione only in 1921. Almost every street, square and embankment road in it carries a dated council act in Roma Capitale's own toponymy register, and this guide quotes those acts rather than guidebooks. The stops are a colossal courthouse, a caryatid fountain, two neo-Gothic churches and a museum of the souls in Purgatory.

sections.heading: How Prati was made
sections.body: The ground was the Horti Domitii, later the Prata Neronis and then the Prata Sancti Petri, and into the 1880s it was an undeveloped flood-plain called Prati di Castello. Italian Wikipedia records that in 1873 the Comune signed a building convention under pressure from Cardinal Francesco Saverio de Mérode, a large landowner here, that the area sat outside the master plan of that year, and that it was folded into the plan of 1883. The Corte di cassazione's own history page gives the frame from the other side: Rome had about 200,000 inhabitants in 1871, and the new quarters built for the capital - it names Prati, Esquilino and Castro Pretorio - went up in a manner contemporaries called piemontese. Fill was trucked in to lift the ground above the Tiber's flood level, and the clay beneath forced repeated consolidation works under the Palazzo di Giustizia. Two aggregators, Italian Wikipedia and Roma Segreta, both give 20 August 1921 as the date of the municipal deliberation that made Prati a rione; no source gives the deliberation itself, so this guide reports the date as theirs. The register corroborates the lateness sideways: its 1914 entry for piazza Cola di Rienzo still reads Q. PRATI, quartiere, while every post-1954 note reads R. PRATI. The rione's arms are blazoned d'azzurro al mausoleo d'Adriano d'argento - Hadrian's mausoleum in silver on blue - which is a building in the neighbouring rione of Borgo, not in this one. Prati's western edge is formed by viale dei Bastioni di Michelangelo and via Leone IV. Both are Italian streets within the rione. Nothing on the far side of the wall belongs to Prati or to any rione.

sections.heading: The street names, and the register that dates them
sections.body: Prati's street list is not an accumulation; it is a programme, written in one go and dated. Roma Capitale's toponymy register carries, for each named public space, every council act that named or re-limited it, with a note giving the rione - which is why this page can date via Cola di Rienzo, piazza Cavour, piazza dei Quiriti, piazza della Libertà and piazza dell'Unità all to one act, Prop. al CC n. 96 of 8 May 1885, and the three embankment roads to acts of 1887 and 1911. The names themselves were drawn from republican and imperial Rome, from the classical writers and from the Risorgimento, and the effect was deliberately anticlerical in a quarter built up against the Vatican wall: Attilio Regolo, Boezio, Caio Mario, Cassiodoro, Catone, Catullo, Cicerone, Crescenzio, Duilio, Ezio, Fabio Massimo, Germanico, Lucrezio Caro, Marcantonio Colonna, Orazio, Ottaviano, Ovidio, Paolo Emilio, Plinio, Pompeo Magno, Pomponio Leto, Properzio, Silla, Tacito, Terenzio, Tibullo, Triboniano, Ulpiano, Varrone, Vespasiano and Virgilio, beside the battle names Damiata, Famagosta, Fornovo, Gavinana, Lepanto, Otranto, Vigliena, Cosseria and Barletta. The register files via Cola di Rienzo under the group Personaggi e avvenimenti storici medioevali e moderni and via dei Gracchi under Antica Roma. The same register records that Prati sits in Municipio I, under Del. AC n. 11 of 11 March 2013, the amalgamation of the municipi, and Del. G. Cap. n. 392 of 8 November 2013. One caution about it: the register publishes a single representative point for each toponym, not a shape, so it settles which acts named a street and not exactly where a long street ends.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Line A of the metro runs along viale Giulio Cesare with two stations inside the rione, Lepanto and Ottaviano. Italian Wikipedia records that both opened on 16 February 1980 with the first Anagnina-Ottaviano section, and that Ottaviano remained the north-western terminus until 29 May 1999, when the line was extended to Valle Aurelia. Ottaviano is often described as serving the rione across the southern boundary; the station itself is in Prati. From the east bank, three bridges land in Prati. Ponte Regina Margherita, of about 103 metres, comes in at piazza della Libertà. Ponte Giacomo Matteotti, 138.6 metres, crosses at the northern corner of the rione. Ponte Pietro Nenni carries line A across the water on its only surface stretch, the tracks rising at via Cesare Beccaria and dropping underground again between viale Giulio Cesare and via degli Scipioni. Roma Capitale records each of these crossings as lying in more than one unit of the city, so none of them is Prati's alone. Via Cola di Rienzo runs the width of the rione from piazza della Libertà at the river to piazza del Risorgimento at the other end.

faq.question: Which rione is Prati, and when did it become one?
faq.answer: Prati is R. XXII, the twenty-second and most recent of the rioni, with the toponymic code 122 in Roma Capitale's Annuario statistico 2022. Italian Wikipedia and Roma Segreta both give 20 August 1921 as the date of the municipal deliberation that constituted it; neither is the act itself. Roma Capitale's toponymy register supports the late date from the side: its 1914 entry for piazza Cola di Rienzo still calls the area a quartiere.

faq.question: Is Prati part of the Vatican?
faq.answer: No. Prati is an Italian rione and Vatican City is a sovereign state that belongs to no rione. Prati's western edge is formed by viale dei Bastioni di Michelangelo and via Leone IV. Both are Italian streets within the rione. Nothing on the far side of the wall belongs to Prati or to any rione. The one embassy building in this guide, the Villino Vivante, houses the Embassy of the Czech Republic; diplomatic premises are inviolable but they are not foreign soil.

faq.question: What are the opening hours of the Carabinieri museum?
faq.answer: The Arma dei Carabinieri states that the museum opens Tuesday to Sunday, 09.00 to 13.00, and closes on Mondays, 1 and 6 January, Easter Sunday and Easter Monday, 1 May, 15 August, 1 November, 8 December, 25 and 26 December. Admission is free. The Arma describes a chronological and thematic route through 26 exhibition rooms, beginning with the Regie Patenti of 13 July 1814.

faq.question: Can you visit the Museo delle anime del Purgatorio?
faq.answer: The museum is one room off the sacristy of the Sacro Cuore del Suffragio, at lungotevere Prati 12. No opening hours and no admission arrangements could be sourced for it: neither the church nor the museum has a website that resolves, so this guide publishes no times. The same applies to the Museo degli orrori at via dei Gracchi 260.

faq.question: Why are all the streets named after Romans and battles?
faq.answer: Because they were named in one programme, not over centuries. Roma Capitale's toponymy register attributes most of the rione's squares and main streets to a single act, Prop. al CC n. 96 of 8 May 1885, and the names were drawn from republican and imperial Rome, the classical writers and the Risorgimento - an anticlerical choice in a quarter laid out along the Vatican wall.

faq.question: Which metro stations serve Prati?
faq.answer: Lepanto and Ottaviano, both on line A, both on viale Giulio Cesare, and both opened on 16 February 1980. Ottaviano was the line's north-western terminus until 29 May 1999. Line A reaches the rione over ponte Pietro Nenni, which carries that line above ground.

photos.title: Palazzo di Giustizia, Tiber front
photos.description: The travertine river front of the Palazzo di Giustizia, seat of the Corte suprema di cassazione, seen head-on from ponte Umberto I, with Ettore Ximenes's bronze quadriga on the attic and the jurist statues along the terrace.
photos.author: Dietmar Rabich

places.name: Palazzo di Giustizia (il Palazzaccio)
places.summary: The seat of the Corte suprema di cassazione, filling the block between piazza Cavour, via Triboniano, via Ulpiano and piazza dei Tribunali, with the public entrance on the piazza Cavour side. Reinforced concrete faced entirely in travertine over more than 27,000 square metres, with a bronze quadriga carrying a winged Victory by Ettore Ximenes on the Tiber front. The building also houses the offices of the Ordine degli avvocati.
places.history: Guglielmo Calderini won the design competition, which Giuseppe Zanardelli chaired. The Court of Cassation states that the first stone was laid on 14 March 1889, in the presence of King Umberto I and Queen Margherita, and that the building was inaugurated on 11 January 1911. Three sources give three different construction spans and this guide publishes neither a start nor an end date beyond those two events. Statues of fourteen jurists stand on the Tiber front and in the cortile d'onore: Giulio Paolo, Quinto Ortensio, Ulpiano, Labeone, Cicero, Gaius, Modestinus, Licinius Crassus, Salvius Julianus, Papinian, Bartolo da Sassoferrato, De Luca, Vico and Romagnosi. The Court's own history records that Calderini, broken by the commission of inquiry into the works, killed himself on 12 February 1916, and gives the crowd's nickname for the building, Palazzaccio, along with the fact that Orson Welles shot part of The Trial here. Italian Wikipedia records that the clay subsoil of the quarter forced repeated consolidation works beneath it. The Ministry of Justice's Biblioteca centrale giuridica is on the ground floor, past the main piazza Cavour entrance. The Court's own history states the library was founded before the unification of Italy, was moved here in 1996 from the ministry's premises in via Arenula into rooms that had originally housed the Corte d'Assise courtrooms, and has been a legal-deposit beneficiary since 1885. The 1889 foundation digging turned up two adjacent sarcophagi, a man and a woman with names of Greek origin, inscribed Crepereius Euhodus and Crepereia Tryphaena. The Corte di cassazione describes an ivory and amber doll among the objects found with Tryphaena, states that her skeleton is today in the Musei Capitolini, and states that the doll's hairstyle allowed archaeologists to date her to the time of the emperor Marcus Aurelius. Rome Art Lover captions its photographs of the sarcophagus and the doll to the Centrale Montemartini. The two accounts disagree and this guide does not choose between them. Roma Capitale's toponymy register carries piazza dei Tribunali under an attribution of 8 May 1885 to rione Prati, confirmed by a limit variation of 1 March 1954.

places.name: Piazza Cavour
places.summary: A square running to via Triboniano, with a planted garden in the middle and the Palazzo di Giustizia along one side. Roma Capitale's register names the streets meeting it: via Crescenzio, via Cicerone, via Tacito, via Lucrezio Caro, via Ulpiano and via Triboniano.
places.history: Roma Capitale's toponymy register records the square under an attribution of 8 May 1885, by Prop. al CC n. 96, with the note R. PRATI. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina, Roma Capitale's own heritage office, states that the central garden was laid out between 1895 and 1911 by Nicodemo Severi. The Waldensian temple and the Cinema Adriano both stand on the square.

places.name: Monumento a Camillo Cavour
places.summary: A bronze, bardiglio marble and granite monument standing in the garden of piazza Cavour, with Cavour in contemporary dress facing the Palazzo di Giustizia. Four colossal bronze groups sit at the foot of the pedestal: Italia and Roma to the south, Pensiero to the west, Azione to the east, and to the north Forza, a lion guarding the urn of the plebiscite.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records the sculptor as Stefano Galletti (1833-1905), the execution as 1885 to 1895, and the unveiling as 24 September 1895, in the presence of King Umberto I, for the twenty-fifth anniversary of 20 September 1870. It gives the two inscriptions: on the south face, A / CAMILLO CAVOUR / ROMA; on the north, XX / SETTEMBRE / MDCCCXCV S.P.Q.R.

places.name: Tempio valdese di piazza Cavour
places.summary: The Waldensian church on piazza Cavour. The congregation's own site states that Sunday worship is at 11.00, and that the Libreria Claudiana is at piazza Cavour, where Laura Ronchi De Michelis's history of the congregation is sold.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia records that the land was bought in 1910 for the Chiesa evangelica valdese by the American Emma Baker, widow of John Stewart Kennedy; that a competition held that year, entered by Arturo Pazzi, by Emanuele Rutelli with Paolo Bonci and by the Turin studio Charbonnet e Cougn, was judged unsatisfactory and rejected ex aequo; and that in January 1911 the commission went to Rutelli and Bonci. The same article dates the building from June 1911 to 1913, credits the interior decoration to Paolo Paschetto and the reinforced-concrete structure to Giovanni Antonio Porcheddu's firm, and gives the inauguration, with a solemn service, as 8 February 1914.

places.name: Teatro Adriano (Cinema Adriano)
places.summary: A Politeama of 1898 on piazza Cavour, now a multiplex cinema. Its operator's information page states only that the cinema opens thirty minutes before the first show and closes thirty minutes after the last, and that opening times vary with the programme.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia records that it opened in 1898 as an opera house to a design by the engineer Pio Rinaldi, and that in the first half of the twentieth century it staged Ponchielli, Puccini, Verdi, Donizetti, Giordano, Leoncavallo, Cagnoni and Mascagni. It was converted to a cinema after the Second World War while continuing to host live events, and was converted to a multiplex in 2000. Italian Wikipedia also reports that the Beatles played here in 1965, on their only Italian tour; that claim rests on that article alone and is repeated here as reported rather than established.

places.name: Chiesa del Sacro Cuore del Suffragio
places.summary: A neo-Gothic parish church on the embankment, by the engineer Giuseppe Gualandi, who took northern Gothic as his model. Italian Wikipedia reports the nickname the building attracted, the little Duomo of Milan. The Museo delle anime del Purgatorio occupies a room off its sacristy.
places.history: The foundation stone was blessed in 1894 by Joseph-Jean-Louis Robert, bishop of Marseille; construction proper began in 1908; the church was consecrated on 17 May 1921. The parish is entrusted to the Missionari del Sacro Cuore di Gesù. Its founder, Victor Jouët, had established the Associazione del Sacro Cuore del Suffragio delle anime del Purgatorio in Rome in 1893. Roma Capitale's toponymy register records lungotevere Prati under an attribution of 1 July 1887, by Prop. al CC n. 166, with the note R. PRATI.

places.name: Museo delle anime del Purgatorio
places.summary: A single room in the sacristy of the Sacro Cuore del Suffragio, holding documents and objects presented as evidence of souls in Purgatory contacting the living. No opening hours and no admission arrangements could be sourced: the church and the museum have no website that resolves, so this guide states none.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia records that a fire in the building on 15 September 1897 damaged a chapel of the Madonna del Rosario, that Victor Jouët read a human face in the scorch marks behind the altar, and that he then travelled Italy, France, Belgium and Germany collecting comparable material. The oldest item is dated 1637. After Jouët's death in 1912, Fr Gilla Vincenzo Gremigni cut the display back in 1921 to what he judged indisputably authentic. The same article names the scorched sleeve of Giuseppe Leleux of Wodecq, whose mother died in 1762 and whose apparition it dates to 1789; the burn-marked garments of Isabella Fornari, abbess of the Poor Clares of Todi, 1731; and a photocopy of a partly burned ten-lire note associated with the monastery of San Leonardo di Montefalco, 1920.

places.name: Piazza dei Quiriti
places.summary: A square off via Cola di Rienzo, running from via Attilio Regolo to via Pompeo Magno, named for the Quirites and built around Attilio Selva's fountain.
places.history: Roma Capitale's toponymy register carries the square under an attribution of 8 May 1885, by Prop. al CC n. 96, and a limit variation of 1 March 1954 noted R. PRATI. The church of San Gioacchino in Prati stands beside it.

places.name: Fontana in piazza dei Quiriti
places.summary: The fountain at the centre of piazza dei Quiriti, named as Roma Capitale names it. A wide low circular basin carries a heavy foliate baluster with projecting bowls; above it a convex basin shaped like a corolla holds four kneeling nude female figures supporting a quatrefoil catino crowned by a monumental pine cone.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records the fountain in piazza dei Quiriti as the work of the Triestine sculptor Attilio Selva (1888-1970), winner of the national competition announced by the Amministrazione capitolina in 1924 for five fountains in five Roman squares in recently built quarters. It dates it 1928, in marble and travertine, originally fed from the Acqua Marcia. It records that the nudity of the four kneeling female figures set off argument first between the sculptor, the Governatorato and Catholic associations, then in the press, delaying an unveiling that had been set for 21 April 1928. The Sovrintendenza gives no replacement date and this guide supplies none.

places.name: Chiesa di San Gioacchino in Prati
places.summary: A parish and titular church beside piazza dei Quiriti, its façade carrying a very large mosaic of the five continents. Italian Wikipedia's official-site field for this church now points to a gambling site and this guide deliberately gives no web address for it.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia and Rome Art Lover both record that the church was built at the wish of Leo XIII to mark his priestly jubilee and dedicated to his baptismal name-saint, that the first stone was laid in 1881, that the works were carried out between 1891 and 1898, that it opened to the public in 1898 and was finished in 1911, and that the architect was Raffaele Ingami. The same sources date the five-continents mosaic to 1898.

places.name: Via Cola di Rienzo
places.address: Via Cola di Rienzo, Roma RM
places.summary: The commercial spine of the rione. Roma Capitale's register states its limits as running from piazza della Libertà to piazza del Risorgimento, and records 272 conforming street numbers on the national address register, certified 16 December 2022.
places.history: The register attributes the street on 8 May 1885, by Prop. al CC n. 96, with the note R. PRATI, and confirms its limits by a determination of 1 March 1954, again R. PRATI. Its caption in the register reads that it is named for Niccolò Gabrini, tribune and senator of Rome of the fourteenth century, and files it under the toponymic group Personaggi e avvenimenti storici medioevali e moderni. Italian Wikipedia gives 1911 as the naming year; the register is the naming authority and this guide follows it.

places.name: Piazza Cola di Rienzo
places.address: Piazza Cola di Rienzo, Roma RM
places.summary: The square where via Cola di Rienzo crosses the piazza Cavour axis, running from via Tacito to via Alessandro Farnese.
places.history: Roma Capitale's toponymy register carries an attribution of 1 January 1914 whose note reads Q. PRATI - quartiere, not rione - and a limit variation of 1 March 1954 noted R. PRATI. That single pair of entries is the best evidence this guide has for how late Prati was constituted a rione: the naming authority was still calling it a quartiere in 1914.

places.name: Piazza dell'Unità
places.summary: A square off via Cola di Rienzo, running to via dei Gracchi, holding the covered neighbourhood market known as the Mercato dell'Unità.
places.history: Roma Capitale's toponymy register carries the square under an attribution of 8 May 1885, by Prop. al CC n. 96, with the note R. PRATI. Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione dates the market building to 1928 and describes it as a twentieth-century neighbourhood market on via Cola di Rienzo; that date comes from that article alone.

places.name: Via Vittoria Colonna
places.summary: A street running from lungotevere Prati to piazza Cavour, carrying Palazzo Blumenstihl at one end and Palazzo Odescalchi Simonetti along it.
places.history: Roma Capitale's toponymy register carries the street under the naming programme of 1885, notes it R. PRATI in the determination of 1 March 1954, and records a variation of its limits by Del. G. Com. n. 404 of 3 December 2008. It is dedicated to Vittoria Colonna, daughter of Fabrizio Colonna and Agnese di Montefeltro. Roma Segreta records that the street was originally called Via Reale.

places.name: Palazzo Blumenstihl
places.summary: An apartment palace with four fronts - via Vittoria Colonna, via Pietro Cavallini, via dei Cosmati 4, where the iron gate is dated 1890, and the grandest on lungotevere dei Mellini. The embankment front has an attic belvedere with a pedimented loggia of three serliane and a long balustraded balcony on four composite columns, forming a triple triumphal entrance. The Gran Caffè Esperia is under that entrance.
places.history: Roma Segreta records that the palace was built in 1890 by the architect Luca Carimini for the Blumenstihl family, of Alsatian origin, who had served the Holy See in the papal army, and that Bernardo Blumenstihl was one of the founders of the Società Italiana per le Condotte d'Acqua. It stands on the site of a theatre destroyed by fire; the sources contradict each other on when that theatre stood and when it burned. Italian Wikipedia names the building as the seat of the Istituto Polacco di Cultura.

places.name: Palazzo Odescalchi Simonetti
places.summary: An apartment palace at the corner of via Pietro Cavallini, four joined blocks around a large courtyard, fronting also via Muzio Clementi and via Marianna Dionigi. Roma Segreta describes a rusticated front with bifore on the first and second floors, and the Odescalchi arms - a crowned black eagle, a passant leopard-lion and six censer-boats - carved on the corner façade.
places.history: It was begun for Prince Baldassarre Ladislao Odescalchi. This guide publishes no architect: the three sources consulted give three incompatible accounts, one crediting Francesco Fontana with a later remodelling by Carlo Busiri Vici, one crediting Fontana with completion by Raffaello Ojetti for the painter Attilio Simonetti, and one crediting Raffaele Ojetti after an 1887 fire at the Odescalchi palace elsewhere in Rome. An unresolved three-way attribution is not settled here by choosing the tidiest version. Italian Wikipedia and Roma Segreta both record that Luigi Pirandello lived in the palace and that his daughter Rosalia was born there.

places.name: Piazza della Libertà
places.summary: A square between via Cola di Rienzo, the embankment and ponte Regina Margherita. Roma Capitale's register gives its limits as running from via Cola di Rienzo to via dei Gracchi. Two separately named public gardens lie inside it, and the Cossa monument stands in front of the bridge.
places.history: The register carries the square under an attribution of 8 May 1885, by Prop. al CC n. 96, with the note R. PRATI, and a limit variation of 1 March 1954 with the same note.

places.name: Giardino Ettore Troilo
places.summary: One of two formally named gardens inside piazza della Libertà. Roma Capitale's toponymy register carries it in its own right, defined as lying within the square; no encyclopaedia article covers it.
places.history: The garden appears in Roma Capitale's register of named public spaces under its own identifier, with the note that it lies all'interno di piazza della Libertà. It is one of the two dedications inside the square that only the municipal register records.

places.name: Giardino Luigi Bigiarelli
places.summary: The second of the two named gardens inside piazza della Libertà, dedicated to Luigi Bigiarelli, the founder of the Società Podistica Lazio.
places.history: Like the Giardino Ettore Troilo, it appears in Roma Capitale's register of named public spaces under its own identifier, noted as lying all'interno di piazza della Libertà, and has no encyclopaedia article. The dedication is the municipal record's.

places.name: Monumento a Pietro Cossa
places.summary: A bronze statue three metres high standing in the garden of piazza della Libertà, in front of ponte Regina Margherita. Everything this guide says about it comes from Roma Segreta: the monument is absent from the Sovrintendenza Capitolina's online index of Roman monuments, so none of it is corroborated by a municipal source.
places.history: Roma Segreta credits the bronze to Adolfo Sanguinetti, cast at the Bastianelli works at San Michele a Ripa, on a pedestal by the architect Bernich, and reports that it was unveiled on 27 September 1895 in what was then piazza S. Elena, today Largo Arenula. The same source reports that the works joining via Arenula to corso Vittorio Emanuele II in the 1920s displaced it, that it was stored inside the Aurelian bastion between Porta San Paolo and Porta San Sebastiano, and that it was moved to piazza della Libertà only in 1962. Pietro Cossa was a Roman dramatist of anticlerical sympathies; his plays include Nerone, Messalina, Giuliano l'Apostata and Cola di Rienzo.

places.name: Museo Storico dell'Arma dei Carabinieri
places.summary: The Carabinieri's own historical museum, on piazza del Risorgimento. The Arma dei Carabinieri states that the museum opens Tuesday to Sunday, 09.00 to 13.00, and closes on Mondays, 1 and 6 January, Easter Sunday and Easter Monday, 1 May, 15 August, 1 November, 8 December, 25 and 26 December. Admission is free. The Arma describes a chronological and thematic route through 26 exhibition rooms, beginning with the Regie Patenti of 13 July 1814.
places.history: The display runs from the founding of the Carabinieri Reali through the Resistance and the Liberation. Italian Wikipedia credits the first published proposal for such a museum to Captain Vittorio Gorini, in the Rivista Militare in 1908, and names Carlo Petitti di Roreto as its founder; both statements rest on that article alone. The building sits on a square Roma Capitale records in two rioni: its toponymy register attributes piazza del Risorgimento to rione Prati on 8 May 1885 and then, in a limit variation of 1 March 1954, notes it R. PRATI E R. BORGO. The museum building itself is in Prati. The Arma gives its address as piazza del Risorgimento without a street number, and this guide does the same.

places.name: Casa Madre dei Mutilati ed Invalidi di Guerra
places.address: Largo dei Mutilati ed Invalidi di Guerra, Roma RM
places.summary: The headquarters building of the Associazione Nazionale Mutilati e Invalidi di Guerra, on a triangular plot: fortress-like, faced in rough tufa blocks with travertine dressings, closed at one end by a tower. Its portal on the embankment side carries the inscription ASSOCIAZIONE NAZIONALE MUTILATI E INVALIDI DI GUERRA and the date MCMXXXVI, three helmeted marble heads, and a Savoy cross whose flanking fasci were removed in 1945.
places.history: Roma Segreta records that the building was commissioned by Carlo Delcroix, president of the ANMIG, built by the Ditta Igliori to a design by Marcello Piacentini in two campaigns, the first block between 1925 and 1928 and a second added in 1936, and inaugurated while still unfinished on 4 November 1928 before King Vittorio Emanuele III and Queen Elena, on the tenth anniversary of the armistice. The same source records that the ANMIG formed spontaneously in 1917 and had half a million members by the mid-1920s. The address is a toponym of its own: Roma Capitale's register created the Largo dei Mutilati ed Invalidi di Guerra on 26 October 1989, by Del. CS n. 2444, out of lungotevere Castello, of which it had until then been an integral part, and dedicated it in memoria di tutti gli invalidi e mutilati di tutte le guerre. The largo is in Prati.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria del Rosario in Prati
places.summary: A neo-Gothic parish church on via degli Scipioni, entrusted to the Dominicans, with an iron gate to the street and a mosaic rose window. Italian Wikipedia's official-site field for this church now serves a gambling landing page, and this guide gives no web address for it.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia credits the design to Giuseppe Ribaldi, dates the completion to 1912-16 and records that it has been a parish since 1912.

places.name: Chiesa della Beata Vergine Maria del Carmine
places.summary: A neo-Renaissance church built for the Carmelites of the monastery attached to it. Its plain façade is inscribed Mater decor Carmeli; inside, three aisles and a polychrome window over the high altar showing the Virgin of Carmel giving the scapular to St Simon.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia dates the building to 1925 and credits it to the architect Edmond Saint Just.

places.name: Cappella di Santa Maria Assunta
places.summary: The neo-Romanesque chapel of the Suore di San Giovanni Battista, annexed to the Santa Maria del Rosario parish and often wrongly called San Giovanni Battista ai Prati after the sisters' name.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia records that the convent and its large school were founded in 1909, and that the congregation itself was founded by St Alfonso Maria Fusco in 1878. This guide publishes no construction date for the chapel: the span the article gives is not consistent with either of those two foundation dates, and no second source settles it.

places.name: Cappella di Santa Maria Immacolata dell'Istituto Scolastico Nazareth
places.address: Via Cola di Rienzo 140, Roma RM
places.summary: A neo-Gothic chapel inside a working school. It is not a building a visitor can walk into from the street, and this guide records it as part of the school rather than as an open church. It belongs to the Sacro Cuore parish.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia credits the Nazareth complex to Corrado de Rossi Re, dates its construction to 1887-1892, and records the chapel's consecration in 1892.

places.name: Villino Cagiati
places.summary: One of the four surviving detached houses of the first Prati, at the corner of via dei Gracchi and via Virginio Orsini. Its façade was restored in the twenty-first century, keeping much of the original metal, stone and ceramic ornament.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia credits the house to the architect Garibaldi Burba and names Giulio Cagiati as the man it was built for. This guide gives no construction date: Italian Wikipedia and Rome Art Lover give dates more than a decade apart and nothing reached settles which is right.

places.name: Villino Macchi di Cellere
places.summary: A detached house at the corner of via Marcantonio Colonna, with 1904 carved on the viale Giulio Cesare façade. It began as a three-storey main block on the viale with a secondary block on via Marcantonio Colonna crowned by a square turret; a floor was later added to both.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia credits the house to Garibaldi Burba, the same architect as the Villino Cagiati, and records that it was built in 1904 for the diplomat Vincenzo Macchi di Cellere.

places.name: Villino Vitale
places.summary: A neo-Renaissance and Liberty house at the corner of via dei Gracchi. Its main façade, with a loggia and a first-floor balcony, faces a garden.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia dates the house to 1900, credits the design to Arturo Pazzi with the engineer Emilio Albertini, and names Felice Giacomo Vitale as the man it was built for. It began as two storeys and a tower and was raised by two more storeys in 1909.

places.name: Villino Vivante
places.summary: A three-storey Liberty house at the corner of via Alessandro Farnese. The building houses the Embassy of the Czech Republic. Diplomatic premises are inviolable under international law, but they are not foreign territory: this is Italian ground, and nothing here is Czech soil.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia credits the house to the engineer Carlo Pincherle, built for Cesare Vivante. This guide gives no construction date: the same article carries two dates three years apart and does not reconcile them.

places.name: Museo degli orrori di Dario Argento (Profondo Rosso Store)
places.summary: A shop opened by the director Dario Argento, with a small museum in the basement reached by a spiral stair. The shop's own site establishes the address and carries a Museo degli Orrori di Dario Argento section. No opening hours could be sourced and this guide states none.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia describes the basement as a single corridor with barred alcoves holding props and creatures from Dèmoni, Phenomena, La chiesa and La sindrome di Stendhal, with reconstructed set pieces.

places.name: Forno pasticceria Angelo Colapicchioni
places.summary: A bakery and pastry shop on via Tacito. Roma Capitale's tourism service lists Forno pasticceria Angelo Colapicchioni, via Tacito 76/78, among the members of the Associazione dei Negozi Storici di Eccellenza, an association founded in 2008.
places.history: No source states more than that municipal entry: not its opening hours, not how long it has traded, nor by whom it has been run.

places.name: Lungotevere Prati
places.summary: One of the three embankment roads wholly inside the rione, running from via Ulpiano to via Vittoria Colonna and carrying the Sacro Cuore del Suffragio at no. 12.
places.history: Roma Capitale's toponymy register attributes it on 1 July 1887, by Prop. al CC n. 166, with the note R. PRATI, and confirms the note in the determination of 1 March 1954.

places.name: Lungotevere dei Mellini
places.summary: The middle embankment road, from via Vittoria Colonna to piazza della Libertà, carrying the grandest front of Palazzo Blumenstihl.
places.history: Roma Capitale's toponymy register attributes it under the same act as lungotevere Prati, Prop. al CC n. 166 of 1 July 1887, with the note R. PRATI.

places.name: Lungotevere Michelangelo
places.summary: An embankment road of the rione, from piazza della Libertà to piazza delle Cinque Giornate.
places.history: Roma Capitale's toponymy register attributes it on 8 May 1911, by Prop. al CC n. 148, with the note R. PRATI, and confirms the note in the determination of 1 March 1954. A fourth embankment road runs on beyond these three; the register places it in two rioni and this guide does not claim it.

places.name: Ponte Regina Margherita
places.summary: A masonry bridge of about 103 metres, some 21 metres wide, landing on the Prati side at piazza della Libertà. Roma Capitale records the bridge as lying in two rioni, Campo Marzio and Prati, and this guide does not present it as Prati's alone.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia dates its construction to 1886-1891 and credits it to Angelo Vescovali, and records that it was first called ponte al Popolo.

places.name: Ponte Pietro Nenni
places.summary: A bridge of three reinforced-concrete spans, 25.4 metres wide, carrying line A of the Rome metro across the Tiber at the surface. The far bank is in Q. I Flaminio, and this guide does not present the crossing as Prati's alone.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia dates the works to 1969-1972, credits the design to Luigi Moretti with Silvano Zorzi, and gives 1980 as the year of inauguration. The metro tracks surface at via Cesare Beccaria and dive again between viale Giulio Cesare and via degli Scipioni.

places.name: Ponte Giacomo Matteotti
places.summary: A bridge of 138.6 metres, 20.1 metres wide, at the northern corner of the rione. Roma Capitale's register notes it in three units - rione Prati, Q. Flaminio and Q. della Vittoria - and this guide does not present it as Prati's alone.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia dates its construction to 1924-1929 and credits it to Augusto Antonelli. It was originally called ponte delle Milizie, then ponte del Littorio.

places.name: Lepanto (metro line A)
places.summary: An underground station on line A at the crossing of viale Giulio Cesare with via Lepanto and via Marcantonio Colonna, a single bore with twin tracks and side platforms.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia records that the station opened on 16 February 1980 with the first Anagnina-Ottaviano section of the line, that it was refurbished in 2012 together with Ottaviano, and that the extra-urban bus terminus that used to sit above it was moved to Cornelia in 2005.

places.name: Ottaviano (metro line A)
places.summary: An underground station on line A at the crossing of viale Giulio Cesare with via Ottaviano and via Barletta.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia records that it opened on 16 February 1980 as the north-west terminus of the line, and ceased to be a terminus on 29 May 1999 when the line was extended to Valle Aurelia.

places.name: Villa Altoviti
places.summary: A sixteenth-century suburban villa that stood on the Tiber bank in the Prati di Castello, on ground the rione now covers. It was demolished in 1889 and nothing of it remains above ground.
places.history: Gaspar van Wittel painted the riverside here, and Rome Art Lover reproduces a second Van Wittel view taken from the villa itself, now in the Galleria Palatina; the villa's river portal appears in the paintings. Italian Wikipedia records that the de Mérode consortium bought the estate, along with the surrounding vineyards, after 1870 - the purchase that put this ground into the hands that built the rione.

entries.name: Palazzo di Giustizia (il Palazzaccio)
entries.note: Guglielmo Calderini's travertine-faced block for the Corte suprema di cassazione: first stone laid 14 March 1889, inaugurated 11 January 1911, with Ettore Ximenes's bronze quadriga on the Tiber front.

entries.name: Piazza Cavour
entries.note: Nicodemo Severi laid out the central garden between 1895 and 1911; the Waldensian temple and the Teatro Adriano both stand on the square.

entries.name: Monumento a Camillo Cavour
entries.note: Stefano Galletti executed it between 1885 and 1895, with four colossal bronze groups at the foot of the pedestal, and it was unveiled on 24 September 1895 for the twenty-fifth anniversary of 20 September 1870.

entries.name: Tempio valdese di piazza Cavour
entries.note: Built from June 1911 to 1913 by Emanuele Rutelli with Paolo Bonci, decorated inside by Paolo Paschetto and inaugurated on 8 February 1914; Sunday worship is at 11.00.

entries.name: Chiesa del Sacro Cuore del Suffragio
entries.note: The engineer Giuseppe Gualandi took northern Gothic as his model on the embankment; the foundation stone was blessed in 1894 and the church consecrated on 17 May 1921.

entries.name: Museo delle anime del Purgatorio
entries.note: One room off the sacristy holding what Victor Jouët gathered across Italy, France, Belgium and Germany after a fire in the building on 15 September 1897, including burn-marked garments of 1731 and 1789.

entries.name: Fontana in piazza dei Quiriti
entries.note: Attilio Selva's marble and travertine work of 1928: four kneeling nude figures hold a quatrefoil catino crowned by a pine cone, and the argument over them delayed the unveiling set for 21 April 1928.

entries.name: Chiesa di San Gioacchino in Prati
entries.note: Built at the wish of Leo XIII for his priestly jubilee, with works carried out between 1891 and 1898 and a mosaic of the five continents of 1898 across the façade.

entries.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria del Rosario in Prati
entries.note: The rione's second neo-Gothic church, entrusted to the Dominicans, a parish since 1912 and completed 1912-16 to Giuseppe Ribaldi's design, with a mosaic rose window behind its iron street gate.

entries.name: Via Cola di Rienzo
entries.note: The shopping street crosses the whole rione from piazza della Libertà to piazza del Risorgimento, carrying 272 conforming street numbers on the national address register, certified 16 December 2022.

entries.name: Palazzo Blumenstihl
entries.note: Luca Carimini built it in 1890 for a family of Alsatian origin; its lungotevere dei Mellini front carries an attic loggia of three serliane over a balustraded balcony on four composite columns, with the Gran Caffè Esperia beneath.

entries.name: Casa Madre dei Mutilati ed Invalidi di Guerra
entries.note: Marcello Piacentini's rough tufa and travertine building for Carlo Delcroix's association, first block 1925 to 1928 and a second added in 1936, inaugurated unfinished on 4 November 1928.

entries.name: Museo Storico dell'Arma dei Carabinieri
entries.note: Free admission, Tuesday to Sunday 09.00 to 13.00, on a route through 26 rooms that begins with the Regie Patenti of 13 July 1814 and runs to the Resistance and the Liberation.

entries.name: Forno pasticceria Angelo Colapicchioni
entries.note: A bakery and pastry shop at via Tacito 76/78, listed by Roma Capitale's tourism service among the members of the Associazione dei Negozi Storici di Eccellenza.

links.note: The Corte di cassazione's history page names Prati, Esquilino and Castro Pretorio together as the quarters built for Rome after 1871.
Sallustiano, like Prati, is in Municipio I; its plots north of via Boncompagni were subdivided out of the Villa Ludovisi estate from 1883.
Ludovisi was built out of the Villa Ludovisi estate, subdivided from 1883 - the same decade in which Prati's grid was laid out and named.
A three-day Rome itinerary. Its metro connections run on line A, whose Ottaviano and Lepanto stations are both in Prati.
